coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
coursesExamined.contribution: Mandatory academic/personal formation, research literacy and civic engagement.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. coursesExamined.name: Behavioral Economics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
coursesExamined.contribution: Uses psychological insights to examine biases, heuristics and framing in economic decisions. Experiments develop understanding of how actual behaviour differs from traditional predictions. This specifically complements empirical customer decisions and adoption; it is not user-interface design.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. coursesExamined.name: Consumer Product Design
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
coursesExamined.contribution: Investigates existing product mechanisms and environmental impact, interviews customers, translates needs into specifications, selects concepts and develops production plans and feasible prototypes. The final product project considers industrial scaling and elementary economics; material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity are explicit. This is a direct design contribution, without a multi-year studio claim.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.

coursesExamined.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies marketing, consumer psychology, qualitative/quantitative insights and responsible engagement. Projects analyse strategy, design a brand and investigate consumer behaviour; customer journeys lead to recommendations. This specifically supports customer value and adoption, not physical-product form-giving.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.

coursesExamined.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.

Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

coursesExamined.name: International Business & Governance
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
coursesExamined.contribution: Analyses international trade, investment, political/sociocultural/technological conditions, governance and responsibility. A market-entry strategy and tariff negotiation case provide specific organisational implementation constraints on the circular-transition direction; it is not technical product design.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.

coursesExamined.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
coursesExamined.contribution: Uses design thinking to identify customer needs, define problems, generate and prototype solutions and build value propositions/business models. A startup plan, pitch and simulation add practical entrepreneurial development. It supplies real product/service concept work, not a dedicated industrial-design studio.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.

coursesExamined.name: Research Methods & Statistics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops empirical research design, measurement, sampling, surveys, experiments and basic statistical inference, followed by an actual team data-collection/analysis project under ethics/privacy rules. These methods complement customer and behavioural inquiry; a design-specific topic is not guaranteed.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

coursesExamined.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies motivation, teams, leadership, conflict, structure, culture and organisational change. Research plans and systematic literature review develop evidence-based organisational inquiry relevant to implementing innovation; no design-management studio is assumed.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

coursesExamined.name: Software Development
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops software-construction skills through C++ and functional programming in Haskell, alongside software design and quality assurance. C++ work addresses classes, inheritance, polymorphism and memory management; Haskell introduces functions, recursion, types and input/output. Laboratories apply version control, code review, debugging, testing, documentation and design patterns. Projects require students to build and explain programs in both languages.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance through discussions and code reviews.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops C++ and Haskell program construction, software design, version control, code review, debugging, testing and documentation through projects. These are actual digital-construction methods, without a guaranteed product interface or deployment/maintenance lifecycle.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Covers software design, creation, testing and maintenance. Uses C++ and Haskell and covers planning, requirements gathering, testing, deployment and maintenance through discussions and code reviews.

coursesExamined.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies data structures, sorting/searching/graph and string algorithms, complexity and computability, with experimental performance investigations. It supplies specific computational design/evaluation methods for digital functions, not industrial form design.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Data Science
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops importing, cleaning, transforming, joining and visualising tabular/text/spatial data in R, plus scraping and a research project. It supplies concrete customer/impact-data analysis methods; no prescribed design dataset is assumed.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

coursesExamined.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
coursesExamined.contribution: Removed from the active selection: generic image-processing methods are real, but Linear Algebra supplies the stronger missing mathematical preparation for robotics.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Image Processing & Computer Vision studies how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognise structures and objects. Topics include colour, image statistics, filtering, segmentation, feature detection, tracking and object classification. Practical work uses Python and OpenCV to develop and benchmark an image-recognition pipeline on previously unseen images.

coursesExamined.name: Robotics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies computational problems in robot motion and manipulation, supported by linear algebra, calculus and geometric modelling. Students analyze forward and inverse kinematics, configuration spaces, collision-free motion planning and grasping, with shorter introductions to sensing and control. Practical work programs a robot arm and gripper; research investigates inverse kinematics for an articulated structure. A smaller component examines a chosen legal, ethical, safety or human-robot issue.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies robot kinematics, configuration spaces, motion planning, collision avoidance and grasping. Programming a robot arm/gripper is actual physical-system computational practice. It supports intelligent product functionality without being an electronics, manufacturing or interface-design sequence.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Programming
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops Python computational problem-solving, data collections, functions, recursion, object-oriented programming, testing and debugging through exercises/projects. It supplies concrete construction skills for computational product functionality, without assuming interface design.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

coursesExamined.name: Mathematical Methods
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops single-variable calculus, complex numbers, integration and differential equations, with Mathematica and an adapted dynamic-model project. It supplies calculus; vectors and matrices are supplied separately by Linear Algebra.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

coursesExamined.name: Linear Algebra
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops vectors, matrices, linear transformations, eigenvalues, orthogonality, least squares and singular value decomposition, with applications and Mathematica. It supplies substantive mathematical foundations for computational motion/robotics after calculus.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Linear Algebra studies systems of equations, matrices, vectors, linear transformations and vector spaces. Students examine eigenvalues, orthogonality, least-squares approximation, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis, with Mathematica supporting analytical problem-solving.

coursesExamined.name: Building with Nature
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies ecological infrastructure interventions in coasts, rivers, cities and ports; projects formulate a Building with Nature intervention and explore constructed walls. It adds actual system/intervention-design practice concerning environmental impacts, without being a consumer-product studio.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.

coursesExamined.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies solar-panel recycling, e-waste metal recovery and plant/mycelium remediation through extensive laboratory work, leaching protocols, concentration/recovery analysis and microscopy. It supplies direct end-of-life material and process investigation, not design engineering by title alone.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

coursesExamined.name: Governance of Sustainability
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
coursesExamined.contribution: Examines institutional power, participation, justice and public/market/civil-society decisions in sustainability. An actual Zeeland issue, expert consultation and policy advice/evaluation provide a specific implementation/governance contribution to circular transitions.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

coursesExamined.name: Sustainability Essentials I
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
coursesExamined.contribution: Introduces planetary boundaries and physical/chemical/thermodynamic sustainability principles. An iterative biopolymer laboratory makes and tests strength/elasticity to improve a formulation. This is a direct material-experiment contribution to circular products as well as environmental foundations.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

coursesExamined.name: Sustainability Essentials II
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops wave physics, chemistry, microscopic structure and macroscopic stress/strain with practical work. coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.

coursesExamined.name: Climate Change
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies climate processes, impacts, mitigation/adaptation, justice, governance and communication; a stakeholder interview and short film connect science to public responses. This specifically frames the environmental transition problems, without implying a mobility-design project.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

coursesExamined.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
coursesExamined.contribution: Assesses environmental, social, health and economic consequences across product/process/service life cycles. Three preliminary projects and an integrated life-cycle assessment directly develop product evaluation and circular-economy reasoning.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.

coursesExamined.name: Calling Bullshit
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines misinformation through philosophy, history, psychology and practical information evaluation. Students distinguish misleading discourse from related concepts, investigate cognitive and social vulnerabilities, and analyze pseudoscience, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact-checking, deepfake production and response exercises develop recognition and intervention skills. Projects map a misinformation narrative's actors and circulation and produce a research-grounded myth-debunking video with an external interview.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies misinformation, cognitive/social vulnerabilities, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact checking, narrative mapping and a research-based debunking video develop specific methods for assessing misleading sustainability claims.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.

coursesExamined.name: Energy & Sustainability
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies renewable-energy resources, conversion technologies and their integration into sustainable energy systems. Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass resources are evaluated through physical principles, resource availability and generation potential. Storage, electricity grids and demand management connect individual technologies to system reliability. Quantitative exercises, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work develop the ability to assess energy options in practical environmental and economic contexts.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies renewable resources, conversion, storage, electricity grids and demand management, with quantitative work, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work. It provides actual energy-system investigation for environmental product/transition choices, not a guaranteed consumer-product project.

coursesExamined.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
coursesExamined.contribution: Removed from the active selection: partner research is real but only offered in semester1 before useful foundations; renewable-energy study supplies a better sequenced circular contribution.

coursesExamined.name: Ethics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops moral reasoning through historical/contemporary ethical theories, close reading and independent research essays. It supplies normative tools for responsible design choices; prescribed environmental/future-generation topics are not assumed.

coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.

coursesExamined.contribution: Introduces psychological/neuroscientific behaviour, neural signalling, learning, personality and social influence. It supplies the actual foundation for Perception & Action and behavioural inquiry rather than ergonomics.

coursesExamined.name: Social Psychology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies social cognition, influence, groups and attitudes with empirical-article analysis and a proposed feasible study. It informs social responses to products, communication and adoption; the final project proposes rather than conducts an experiment.
coursesExamined.descriptionRead: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

coursesExamined.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops multivariable models, comparisons of means, categorical outcomes and latent constructs with R analysis, assumption checks, papers and a poster. This specifically supports the evaluation of behavioural/customer evidence, without assuming a product-testing project.

coursesExamined.name: Persuasive Communication
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.

academicJudgment: Retain two related-fields comparisons after a fresh programme-level challenge. The defining subject is designing products/services/systems that integrate user needs, technology, organisational viability and consequences. UCR Consumer Product Design directly performs that integration through customer interviews, specifications, concept selection, production/prototyping and economic/environmental evaluation. Entrepreneurship adds actual need/problem/prototype/value/business-model work; Marketing adds brand design and customer journeys; Market Research conducts empirical customer inquiry; LCA performs integrated product/process assessment. Those recurring, documented product/user/value questions connect the complements to the target. The digital direction adds actual software construction and programmed robot-arm manipulation, while behavioural perception, decision experiments, empirical methods and organisational strategy address human/organisation dimensions. The circular direction adds iterative biopolymer testing, material structure/properties, actual recovery laboratories, renewable-energy experiments, energy-option assessment and governance inquiry. This is stronger than generic business, computing or environmental coherence with one nominal matching title. It is also narrower than Delft’s cumulative industrial-design formation. Missing full studios, ergonomics, CAD and manufacturing progression remain material limits, but do not negate these documented related product-development inquiries. No matching-course quota, full-equivalence or licence test is used. Partner project topics and digital/robotic assignments are not assumed to be industrial products or interfaces. Their actual construction/research skills and explicitly product-centred anchors, not imaginary projects, support the comparison.
descriptionOnly: Market Research, Perception & Action, Strategy & Digital Transformation, Renewable System Design and other description-only evidence receive full consideration within the supplied substance. No course is dismissed for lacking enrichment. Selected source/provenance distinctions stay internal. DISCOMP213 official description supports its unchanged shared modal text; the case contribution conservatively uses the detailed current construction evidence. No new shared-description defect inferred.

otherPortfolioLeads.evidenceRead: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
otherPortfolioLeads.finding: Actual interviews, ethnography and qualitative analysis are a valid additional user-method lead. Existing empirical/market/behaviour work supplies adequate specific inquiry; this lead does not by itself establish an additional design direction or mandated replacement.

otherPortfolioLeads.evidenceRead: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
otherPortfolioLeads.finding: Actual documentary production provides visual representation and interviewing, but it does not establish industrial visualisation/form-giving or a sustained UX direction.

otherPortfolioLeads.evidenceRead: Explores spatial engineering and geospatial technologies like GIS and remote sensing for addressing global challenges such as natural disasters, food shortages, resource decline and pollution. Emphasises hands‑on projects in disaster response, sustainable agriculture and environmental monitoring.

otherPortfolioLeads.evidenceRead: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
otherPortfolioLeads.finding: Actual behavioural experiments now support user/customer decisions in the closest programme; they do not alone create a separate health or interaction-design programme.

alignmentFinding: All34selectedcodes and25externalcomponents appear exactly once across blocks. Partial relationships retained for product design, research/customer methods, people, organisations, digital strategy, data, robotics, impacts and values. Dedicated design theory, interfaces, product engineering, repeated studios and choice/minor spaces remain visible gaps. Optional15EC independent research appears only as a comparison row once per UCR programme, not in scheduled180EC; it does not claim a guaranteed industrial-design final project.
stopping: Two alternatives retained after evidence, coherence, qualitative/numerical distinctness and feasibility. Health, mobility and digital-interaction candidates assessed separately and rejected on their actual design contributions; no quota or default third alternative.
qualitativeDistinctness: Ten courses/75EC differ in each direction. The first’s programming, calculus/linear algebra, algorithms/software, data and robot motion plus perception provide actual digital/human-function inquiry. The second’s material sciences, climate/communication, recovery laboratories, energy assessment and governance implement circular-transition questions. Both keep direct product/customer methods. This is substantive choice, not a threshold-filling swap.
